speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These include healthcare workers and patients, lower income families and SMEs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This amount was funded by voluntary contributions from Keppel's directors and staff, and dollar-for-dollar matching by Keppel.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Our local aviation firms, such as SIA, Jetstar Asia and SATS have also leaned forward to facilitate interested workers to help out in public services that require surge capacity during this period.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Vloggers and bloggers are helping to share public messages.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Others are volunteering, giving support and encouragement and, crucially, by complying with health advisories and practising safe distancing.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: These include foreigners who live amongst us and who care deeply about Singapore.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Many have also had to make sacrifices in this time.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: Families have had to make difficult adjustments to their lives, some having to undergo quarantine, cancel celebrations or put off long-awaited plans, including wedding plans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And despite our best efforts to work with businesses and unions to save jobs, some workers have suffered a loss of income or jobs.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The Government and the political leadership are in this with Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We share the worries and anxieties of Singaporeans, and we will do our best for you.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will walk with every Singaporean, through every up and down.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: To show solidarity with Singaporeans, I announced at the Budget Debate last month that the political leadership will take a one-month pay cut.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: With the deteriorating situation, we will go further.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: All Political Office Holders will take an additional pay cut of two months – altogether a three-month cut in their salary.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: And we must all look after one another in these trying times.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will stand with one another, through thick and thin.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is what it means to be SG United.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is what it means to be Singapore Together.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: The months ahead will not be easy as the situation continues to evolve dynamically and unpredictably.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will protect and advance the well-being and livelihoods of Singaporeans.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will stand with our fellow Singaporeans to look out and care for one another at a time of fear and anxiety.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: We will work with our people and institutions around the world to combat this global threat.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the essence of who we are as a nation.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: This is the essence of who we are as a people.

speaker: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance (Mr Heng Swee Keat)
text: I am confident that, together, we will ride through this storm and emerge even stronger.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Deputy Prime Minister, I believe you have something more to say.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Since then, almost on a daily basis, we hear of grim updates of worsening situations about the number of cases spiking up, more lockdowns and restrictions around us, around the world, and economies and markets in a near meltdown state.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The next one month will be critical in our fight.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The health and well-being of Singaporeans must come first.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Hence, the necessary and painful further measures added on, which would understandably impact our lives and also further disrupt businesses.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I fear the worst is yet to come, with more businesses at risk of failing and more jobs at risk of being lost.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must do our best to stem this economic contraction, if not, slow that economic shrinkage.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In other words, 2020 will be a year of recession.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: GDP growth essentially is computed by aggregating the outputs in consumption or C, I for investment or I, the trade export less import or X minus I, and finally, Government spending or G.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the still deteriorating situation, the unprecedented restrictive measures as well as uncertainties ahead, we can expect consumption, investments and exports to decrease sharply, contracting the overall GDP.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The only component that can shore up the economy now is G – Government spending.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And since February, we have seen the Government introducing three heavy doses of Budget support measures, including today's announcement of further expansions of measures to prop up the GDP.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We have to utilise a combination of both the current reserves from this term of Government and a draw from the past reserves to fund the various packages.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having this financial strength and capacity to inject massive spending into the economy in this time of need, yet without straining our fiscal balance sheet, is most reassuring.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It instills confidence and puts us in good stead to continue attracting investments and trade.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It also reassures Singaporeans that the Government has the financial capacity to fight the COVID outbreak and take care of Singaporeans so that our people are not in a state of fear, which could otherwise result in further cut back in consumption and other social consequences.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Also, importantly, our strong accumulated past reserves guarantee us the resource to stabilise and rebuild our economy and thereafter, engineer new growth areas again when the crisis is over.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Thanks to the decades of careful financial management, today, we are able to deal with this crisis in a position of financial strength.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have been in the Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) for Finance and Trade and Industry since I became a Member of Parliament in 2006.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The reason I choose to serve in this GPC is because I truly believe that financial prudence and discipline will safeguard Singapore, and I want to do my part in Parliament to uphold this key foundational principle.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The GPC for Finance must be the guardian of financial prudence and discipline.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To me, financial prudence and discipline are not just ideological beliefs but real and necessary adherence so as to ensure our continuing existence as a country.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Over the years of Budget debates and speaking about financial prudence in this House, I often do get critiques or even ridicules from some quarters that say that I am too conservative in my views and that the Government is already building too much buffer in our financial management.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I actually think it is always good to err on the safe side when it comes to the country's finances.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Even if we did indeed over-save, the investment returns of our excess savings will still be ploughed back to fund the current Budget through our Net Investment Returns Contribution (NIRC).

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In Singapore's context, we actually need a higher factor of safety financially, so to speak, just so that we have the financial capacity to rebuild and restore our entire economy again should a catastrophic event happen in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The direct cash wage subsidies are still the most practical way to save jobs and to help companies with their cash flow problems.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It has worked for us before during the financial crisis and helped us save jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Given the deteriorating situation, the timeliness of the assistance packages and the measures becomes more crucial.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to have it sooner rather than later, as has been expressed in the Resilience Budget as well as today's Solidarity Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The substantially increased support to the most badly affected sectors like aviation and tourism in the Resilience Package are most necessary to help save jobs as they are really being directly hit by the impact of COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Although, very sadly, some workers may inevitably be laid off or see their incomes significantly reduced.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Kudos to the Government for going that extra mile to ensure that assistance is paid out in the month of April.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I have been following Minister Desmond Lee's Facebook page very closely in the last one week.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: He has given very reassuring and timely updates on how Singaporeans can apply for the TRF and thereafter, the COVID-19 Support Grant, among the many schemes.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am also heartened that MSF has agreed to be flexible and to be sympathetic in approving the applications and also to expedite the $500 payout, such as by using PayNow.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With most workplaces shut down and distancing measures in place, I hope that the job placement efforts would not be severely curtailed and I hope that the agencies continue to work on helping workers find jobs.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I am also glad that the Government has not forgotten the self-employed Singaporeans who are also badly affected by the crisis and has extended assistance them, and as of today, we have extended the package as well.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Self-Employment Person Income Relief Scheme is a good start.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It is always difficult to devise a new scheme from scratch and all in a short span of time.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Self-employed persons come from a wide range of circumstances, and hence whatever is the criteria set, there will be some who do not meet the criteria or fall through the gaps.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I must say I received the most queries on this scheme from my residents since the scheme was announcement on 26 March.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: While I am glad the scheme has been further improved and enhanced, I hope that MOF and MOM can continue to fine-tune this scheme with the aim to include more self-employed Singaporeans who are in need of the assistance.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, cash flow is the most critical and immediate concern.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The various cash flow support assistance whether is via the JSS, Wage Credit Scheme or the deferment of income tax payments can help ease the pain.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I appreciate that MOF is now doing their best to flow the payouts to companies sooner, as soon as in the month of April.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I hope the MOF can also fast-track the later tranches of the JSS earlier, if possible to July and August instead of paying the final tranches in October.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The sectors that are severely affected like aviation and tourism would badly need the cash assistance sooner rather later.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such public-private partnership to avail credit can have a multiplying effect and move the needle in providing risk capital which can be used to develop opportunistic and new-to-economy capabilities.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Having such forward-looking investments, even during a crisis, bodes well when the recovery does come.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I will conclude with a few questions for the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, it is also important in this debate that we articulate and establish the basis and the justification of our strong actions and also the proportionality of it.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to ask the Deputy Prime Minister if he can set out the basis and rationale for our fiscal responses so far, and how is this crisis different from past crises?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The Government has implemented a series of measures since January and many Singaporeans are trying hard to adapt, to adjust to the new restrictions and measures.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The outbreak may actually get worse before it gets better.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: And there is no certainty how long this will take.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Financial assistance aside, how could we help Singaporeans cope with this crisis better, especially with the circuit breaker we put in place and enforced?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: How can we help Singapore cope and respond better to this crisis?

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We now have the Unity Budget, the Resilient Budget and the Solidarity Budget.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: There may well be further Budget packages depending on how the COVID-19 situation develops, but I believe we will eventually have a Victory Budget in time to come where we position ourselves for a strong recovery and to emerge stronger.

speaker: Mr Liang Eng Hwa (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: So, I would like to hear from the Deputy Prime Minister how he sees Singapore emerging from this crisis once the storm passes.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As we speak, the situation with COVID-19 continues to evolve rapidly in Singapore and in every country around the world.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The impact of COVID-19 on individuals and businesses is unprecedented.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: In just a short span of 10 weeks since the first confirmed case of COVID-19 in Singapore, all our lives have changed dramatically.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How we work, interact, eat and even greet each other has changed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Even standing-in-line has required us to practise safe distancing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The outbreak of COVID-19 and the various measures across countries to prevent the spread of COVID-19 is causing severe economic impact on businesses as channels for the demand for goods and services as well as supply chains have been disrupted and individuals have suffered loss of income, and for some, even their jobs.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While helping our people and business deal with immediate pain, I am glad that the Resilience Budget does also invest in ensuring that Singapore stays resilient and emerges stronger.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Given the sharp drop in business demand and the disruptions to supply chains, the challenge is that businesses may not be able to afford to continue at the same capacity and cost and hence will and may still have some of the jobs impacted and retrenchments may not be avoidable for some of their workers.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Can the Deputy Prime Minister also share how we ensure that businesses get this wage support will continue to hire these workers?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What support will be given to workers if retrenchment is still inevitable?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: But as the Deputy Prime Minister has pointed out, the key is helping people keep their jobs so that livelihoods are not impacted.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do we help people find jobs,especially in today's environment as businesses are shrinking and jobs are going away?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As it is likely that the COVID-19 situation will continue for some time, what is crucial is that the economy does not come to a standstill.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: It is timely that the Resilience package and the Solidarity Budget are providing training and income support for also the self-employed persons (SEPs) as they too have been impacted quite severely.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Ultimately, though, we must still work together to keep the economy going.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While we are fortunate to have strong past reserves that we can draw on to provide the needed relief as well as to prepare workers and businesses for the recovery, unless there is business and economic growth, over the long term, this will not be sustainable.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Therefore, we should all pull together to work to contain this spread so that we can shorten the period and return to normalcy as soon as possible, although the timeline looks like it is going to drag on.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: MOM’s call and measures to support people to work from home and now with the latest circuit breakers, most people will be working from home except for those in essential services.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: There could be, however, individuals and some companies that may not have the resource or be enabled to do so, as they do not have access to capabilities to telecommute.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: What help can be extended to both individuals and businesses to help them with this transition and to enable them to work effectively from home?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For the worker, even if he or she is resourced to work from home, because all of use are working from home on a mass scale, a family’s resources may not be sufficient to meet the needs of everyone all at once.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: As an example, the family may have a notebook, but now that all family members are working from home, they will all be vying for the same resource at the same time.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: The other consideration would be how conducive the environment at home is for everyone.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Just imagine several adults at a home teleconferencing at the same time and then having children trying to do their home-based learning also at the same time in a small space.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: All these will add stress to any home environment.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: While funding is important and necessary, given how quickly things are changing, it takes more than funding and policy to ensure that Singaporeans impacted get the support needed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Equally important is having the right capability and the process to pull together resources to ensure that needs can be met.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To illustrate the point, there are people who because they are either vulnerable or have family circumstances that make it difficult for them to get essential services they need.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How do we ensure that products and services can reach them?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With the surge of demand also for essential services, even if people have the ability to get online for those services, it may be very difficult because now online orders are also overwhelmed.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, how can we provide a way to broker and get resources better connected so that both businesses and individuals who need these services will be able to access them in a timely manner?

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: For example, could we have a portal for people to be able to know what needs are, to sign up and to be able to be activated if their resources or their capabilities are required.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: I am personally concerned for the overall well-being of Singaporeans caused by the anxiety of the COVID-19 outbreak and infection.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Added to this is the stress brought about with safe distancing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: We are social beings and interaction and relationships are important to us.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: To some extent, I do see a silver lining as technology today – while it cannot completely substitute a face-to-face interaction – has allowed us to continue to engage despite the need for safe distancing.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Video-calls and teleconferencing have allowed people to continue to "see" each other as well as to "work with each other" across different locations.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: So, while it is painful, this crisis is also accelerating the need for and driving transformation and change at all levels.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: Individuals and businesses are adopting and adapting to digital technologies and platforms to help them address current constraints and circumstances.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: With COVID-19, many Singaporeans now have experienced and have first-hand understanding of the impact of Singapore’s dependency of imports for our food supply.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: This is an excellent unifying platform to rally Singaporeans for a resilient Singapore.

speaker: Ms Jessica Tan Soon Neo (East Coast)
text: How and when COVID-19 will end is not clear.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Singapore Government has responded in a timely manner and has sought to contain the spread of the virus locally.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Its actions have mitigated and kept the situation largely under control.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Years of preparation, exercises and training in the healthcare realm, in particular, have borne fruit.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: However, a second phase of infections marked by, first, returning Singaporeans and now – by the increased community spread of the disease – has proved more challenging and difficult to manage.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Our workers fighting in the trenches and workers supporting the fight – from nurses to cleaners, from GP doctors to infectious disease specialists, from medical researchers to delivery persons, and those Singaporeans driving our people to hospitals and quarantine facilities – are our heroes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: We should not forget our public officers, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: From civil servants and teachers to those guarding our borders and public spaces, namely, our men and women in uniform, we must honour them for trying to allow Singaporeans to live our lives as normally as possible while keeping us safe.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The same goes for every Singaporean involved in this fight.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: With the world economy practically shut down, the Government – like many others around the world over the last two to three weeks – has responded swiftly with financial support for its citizenry.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For the moment, they are a comprehensive response that will save businesses and jobs and help lower and middle income households tide over the difficult short-term effects of the global economic shutdown.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is good that the assistance quantum and timeframes for the various schemes are calibrated according to the different degrees of vulnerability faced by the target groups.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I acknowledge the support to a group of workers – private-hire bus drivers for whom some specific support and relief was announced by the Resilience Budget.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Such measures do play an important part in mitigating cost-of-living concerns.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I also wish to acknowledge the diligence of public officers, such as those at Enterprise SG, who have sought to engage financial institutions and banks to withhold the repossession of vehicles that our workers need for their livelihood.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The challenge of much of this work – seeking the cooperation of large enterprises and businesses to exercise goodwill can be back-breaking and easily underestimated.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Nonetheless, Sir, it is very likely that some businesses will close, more workers will lose their jobs, and many Singaporeans will face or are already facing pay cuts.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: As Deputy Prime Minister Heng said, the economic effects of the pandemic are likely to be long lasting.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The financial assistance measures in the Resilience Budget, in the main, will be effective for three to nine months.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The questions I have are for the longer term.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I am of the view that this is rightly called a Resilience Budget, because resilience is about being able to take a hit and recovering to continue like before.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if the pandemic is likely to take at least one year to be resolved, how long would the economic effects last?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: What is the Government’s assessment of future scenarios?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This gives much food for thought, not just on questions the Workers’ Party asked in the past, such as the size and usage of our reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: These questions will come to the fore again, and I am grateful for the many Singaporeans who have called for the Workers’ Party to keep pressing for a greater discussion of Singapore’s reserves.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: This remains an eminently reasonable call and embodies the spirit of SG Together with our people seeking information and taking ownership of our society and collective future.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A bifurcation of the world between the US and China that this House was warned about may well accelerate as the world remembers the supply chain effects of COVID-19 on their economies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Separately, consumption in the US and Europe, which drive the world economy to a large extent, has dwindled and many remain hopeful for the pandemic to reach its peak and ease off quickly.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The rest of the developing world are in a lockdown mode.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I believe this mighty storm that we are experiencing is not just something we need to keep safe from by staying at home.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The storm shakes up the very structure of our open economy and threatens its foundation, especially our hub status.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Looking ahead, it could derail and damage our aspiration to be a Global-Asia node of technology, innovation and enterprise.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: NUS Business School Professor Lawrence Loh wrote in a recent commentary that the Resilience Budget is like the New Deal implemented by President Franklin D Roosevelt to rebuild the American economy and society during the Great Depression.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The New Deal took more than six years and secured the US as a welfare state with a strong federal government and a perennial national debt problem.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The comparison with the New Deal is nonetheless thought-provoking.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Indeed, the Resilience and Solidarity Budgets have the features of a New Deal for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For Singaporeans who will continue to see disruption and technology reduce their job prospects, can we expect continued support for them in the nine months after this package expires, particularly for training and wage support, for example?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: If so, what considerations would determine the Government’s thinking on this matter?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, Sir, COVID-19 has thrown up some useful lessons, like all crises do.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: For example, the implications of a COVID-19 type pandemic must have implications on our population and economic plans and strategies.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: COVID-19 has also exposed sectors of the economy that could perhaps be manned by more Singaporean workers in future for better resilience and national outcomes.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A thorough review of what a living wage in Singapore ought to be for Singaporeans who man our critical infrastructure and keep the country’s heart beating would also be appropriate and timely, the same way strengthening our food security and critical supply chains are.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And what about our army of cleaners, both local and foreign, and the local SMEs and cleaning companies that operate in this space?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Singapore owes them a debt of gratitude in this difficult period and it is time our workers who keep Singapore clean are paid far more respectable wages, with Singaporeans ready to play their part, too.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: I do not think many of us truly appreciate how much more work they are doing trying to keep our HDB estates clean while continuing to clear garbage and bulky items, and keeping to their daily routines.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: It is the respect all of us must extend to them and all those who earn an honest living that matters so much in shaping the type of progressive society we aspire to be.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Only then can we say we are a people who leave no one behind.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: After Singapore defeats COVID-19 – and defeat it we will – let us turn our attention, more acutely than ever, back on the Singaporean worker and their families, the reality of inequality and job competition.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: How can they be better protected and not hamstrung by the insecurity to raise a family in the socio-economic context of Singapore?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And, of course, the disturbing news many of us read this morning in The Straits Times on the living conditions of some foreign workers is a stain on Singapore and Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: But if resilience is going to be a longer term issue lasting perhaps even up to five years, and a major restructuring of the economy and society is required, how is the Government going to balance the Budget in the next term of Government?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Would we need to adopt belt-tightening austerity measures to balance the Budget?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: And do we need to adopt a different stance towards the reserves, debt financing and deficits?

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: All these considerations are going to affect the lives of Singaporeans and our political system as well.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: A PAP Government with a fresh five-year mandate given by Singaporeans before the next annual Budget will face an unprecedented problem in recent memory.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The initial period of the term of Government would require extra fiscal prudence and it will also mean less fiscal firepower to deal with the mighty storm of the pandemic and its aftermath.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To conclude, Mr Speaker, in 1971, in a speech to his grassroots leaders, the late Foreign Minister S Rajaratnam spoke of a Democracy of Deeds, where our actions ought to speak louder than our words.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Mr Rajaratnam was wise enough to share with his grassroots leaders that he was not saying that a one-party Parliament was a good thing.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: In this likely prolonged state of economic recession, Parliament will have to focus on a Democracy of Needs.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Today, we are witnessing the threats of a pandemic to both livelihood and life itself.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: So, we must question its long-term impacts on the economic and even psycho-social needs of our citizens.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: Tomorrow, after we defeat COVID-19 – and defeat it we will – we must address the long-term needs of our people in a sustainable and equitable manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: To this end, our reserves and the prospect of taxes should continue to be robustly debated and considered in a detailed manner.

speaker: Mr Pritam Singh (Aljunied)
text: The Workers’ Party will play its role in these debates, which is not just a function of talk, but a key purpose of this House – to determine what is best for this country we call home and our fellow Singaporeans.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This is the global catastrophe of our times.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Singapore and the rest of the world were so different just four months ago.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, the world – or rather, more correctly, humanity – is facing the biggest challenge of our generation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Today, the world is so interconnected with all countries so interdependent on one another for free flow of services, goods and resources.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: It is also not just another thunderstorm, which was just described by Mr Pritam Singh.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: But it is like an Ice Age descending upon the world, suddenly freezing everything in its way – all transportation, human movements and activities.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The impact is not just medical but we can see a larger social and economic and fallout, as the Ice Age recedes later.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We can expect a tsunami of flood waters to follow.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Nature has its unique ways to handle external shocks.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During the seasonal change from autumn to winter, many animals and plants have adapted and developed coping mechanisms.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Many animals such rodents and polar bears go into hibernation mode during winter.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Hibernation functions to conserve energy when sufficient food is not available and when external conditions are hash and unfavourable.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: The animals are able to lower their metabolic rate, lower their temperature, slow down breathing and heart rate to conserve energy.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During this COVID global crisis, how I wish Singapore can just go into a hibernation mode and emerge only later when the global contagion is over.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: When this winter gives way to spring – as it would ultimately – then we are ready to take off and rebuild our economy and our lives again.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: During this period, what are the main worries on most peoples' minds?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are worried for our safety and health.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are worried about how the containment measures will disrupt our lives and livelihoods.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: How our jobs are being affected, how are we going to pay for our daily bills, our mortgages, loans, insurance premiums, utility bills, service and conservancy fees and food?

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And for many employers, they are facing the largest and biggest challenge with revenue plunging sharply and their supply chains disrupted.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: With both supply and demand evaporating suddenly in a short duration of two months, many viable and good businesses may not survive this winter.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I applaud the Government for the quick rescue actions to help the individuals and the businesses with the Unity and Resilient and now the Solidarity Budgets.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: These are targeted to address many of the these concerns.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are immensely grateful to our Pioneers and Merdeka Generations for diligently building up our national reserves which now serves as our hibernation, emergency and survival fuel.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: As this is an unprecedented times, I would like to present a few suggestions to Deputy Prime Minister and our Government to consider.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will also include stopping the mandatory MediSave contributions of self-employed persons (SEPs) including taxi drivers and many others.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Together with the enhanced Job Support Scheme, this will further cushion our employers from manpower cost.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: For the employees and SEPs, it will ease their cash flow.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: I understand the importance and significance of our CPF as it serves as our retirement nest eggs.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Even the Government has to dip into our national reserves to tie us through this crisis.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We can always save again when the crisis is over and when spring is back.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Two, one of the major concerns of stopping CPF contributions is the payment of the HDB housing loans, which many depends on.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: If HDB can grant such an interest free deferment, then CPF Board will be at the losing end.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: So, I would like to suggest the CPF Board to consider a freeze in interest payment to all CPF accounts for the same period.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Last of all, bringing forward the S&CC rebates as well as U Save.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: This will certainly help many HDB households to ease their cash flow.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Our hearts go to all those who have been severely affected by this virus.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: And our prayers and thanks also go to our healthcare workers and other support agencies staff.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: To those whose jobs are on the line, we stand with you and we are here with you.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: We are fighting a war; this is worse than a guerrilla war.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Only by staying together, following the Government's guidelines on social distancing, exercise personal hygiene and stay at home, complying with quarantine orders, then we can overcome this long winter together faster and emerge stronger as a nation.

speaker: Dr Lim Wee Kiak (Sembawang)
text: Everyone of us is on the frontline now and we must play our part.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These measures have made a huge difference in assuring Singaporeans that our Government is taking take care of all of us.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In living with COVID-19, as individuals and businesses, we all have to make huge changes which are often uncomfortable and unprecedented.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: But even as we make these huge changes overnight – and these are changes which would in better times have taken months or years of study and discussion, the devil is always in the details.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Before I carry on my speech, I will like to declare my interest as the CEO of ComfortDelGro Taxi business.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is a classic solution of killing two birds with one stone, addressing the ramped-up demand for grocery and food deliveries, and giving our affected drivers an alternative source of income.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, I am open to all ways that can help our cabbies survive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: However, the puzzle pieces do not automatically click into place.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, cabbies making food deliveries need to park the car in a carpark, wait for the food to be ready which take some time, and drive to a destination which might also charge parking fees.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The key difference between car drivers and delivery people using bicycles or motorcycles, is the parking fees, and the need to find carpark slots which may be unavailable or very far away.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many of my residents, friends and colleagues are complaining that they cannot find a slot for the online grocery companies to deliver their groceries in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many think that these online firms cannot cope with their delivery schedules due to the lack of delivery vehicles.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Thus, urging me to send 10,000 taxis to the rescue.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is so that they can get their groceries ordered online to be delivered on time.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As industries are thrown into states of ramped-up demand versus no demand, there are other situations where "perfect matches" might exist.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Coming back to the topic of online grocery shopping.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: I understand that the long waiting time, of up to a week or two, may not necessarily be due to the lack of delivery personnel, but the lack of people to pick and pack the groceries.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: What about the people in the tourism industry that are without jobs due to almost zero tourist arrival?

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We need e2i and other job agencies, to leverage on existing job portals so that down-and-out Singaporeans can refer to and sign up for temporary jobs which are currently in huge demand.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: COVID-19 is forcing us to make rapid changes.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This need for swift changes can be seen in a good light.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: For example, COVID-19 is accelerating digital transformation and completely overturning the way things may have been done, things which might have taken a far longer period to change otherwise.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Many people, for instance, have to work from home, which bosses might not have liked in the past including myself but there is no choice now.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If a blend of home and office work becomes a more accepted norm, this will improve work-life balance and also traffic congestion in the long run, including easing the public transport on the train or the bus.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This also presents an opportunity for the Government to spend wisely.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Not only as a fiscal stimulus to keep the economy going or put money in citizen's pockets, now $600, but to build up Singapore's future capabilities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: One of these major areas is in digitisation, which has become critical at a time when the only thing that could link us when you are at home for the next one month to the outside world, is our Internet connection.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The learning curve is extremely steep and drastic, yes, but thousands of teachers all over Singapore have no choice but to teach onscreen.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This goes beyond school teachers to those who give tuition, teach musical instruments, even corporate trainers.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We urge them to organise themselves to learn different online learning platforms so that they can use these to survive and perhaps with a nudge from the Government with some funding.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: They need these digital skills now, and they can use these skills even after the COVID-19 threat is over.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Similarly, our fellow Singaporeans selling food at the hawker centres or eating places have to adapt to a new reality come tomorrow, 7 April.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: To better survive, they need to establish an online presence so they can sell to Singapore residents who order through platforms like of Food Panda and others.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: Physical dollars and coins are not the cleanest items to carry around and now is the time to accelerate our cashless push.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: The vulnerability of Singapore's food supplies has never been clearer.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is what I have observed in my recent trip to Israel late last year.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: We have to put deep thoughts into making urban farming scalable and sustainable.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: (In Mandarin):   These are extraordinary times as we fight the COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: These days, we wash our hands often to reduce the chance of infection.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: After the outbreak, this habit will make us healthier.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In the old days, to change a habit may take years, but now, we must change within a few months.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: If we do not change, we will not survive.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: It is often said that a crisis also presents opportunities.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: As long as we stay united with the Government during the outbreak, learn digital technology and embrace the digital economy, the sky will become bluer after the rain.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: This is not a war against another human race but a war against an invisible virus.

speaker: Mr Ang Wei Neng (Jurong)
text: In war time, we must do what we may not like, change in the way we never thought we would, and do whatever we can to help everyone survive.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In a span of two months, the viral outbreak has seen countries, rich and poor, scrambling to come to terms with understanding the health impacts of the disease and how to effectively contain its spread.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Social distancing measures have upturned economic and social activity.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Today, 6 April, is a milestone in Singapore as most businesses prepare to shutter their premises in line with Government directives, something that has not happened in my lifetime.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: What is enough to deal with the impacts of the virus?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: At one level, the health consequences on most people are manageable, with serious consequences falling on mainly the elderly and those with pre-existing conditions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As such, it was recently pointed out by Harvard Prof Michael Sandel that one could theoretically make a choice that economic and social activity should be kept up as only a minority of people would become seriously ill.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, he warns that making that choice would be a purely utilitarian calculation that is detrimental to the common good, as there is a moral dimension that is immutable.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are all members of society and the key question is: "What do we owe one another?" There is also the concern that the healthcare system should not be overwhelmed.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With our own rising caseload from local transmissions, I agree that the circuit breaker directive announced last Friday is necessary.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To ease the economic pain caused by COVID-19, G20 leaders have agreed that governments should utilise available tools to minimise the economic and social impact.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To this end, many governments have announced support packages to help businesses and households.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: That said, we have some questions about how the sums add up and whether some of the monies will go towards achieving their intended purposes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: We are also concerned that large corporations who receive taxpayer help do not engage in irresponsible behaviour once recovery resumes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My other colleagues will speak on some of these aspects.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: My speech today will focus on seeking some clarifications on the measures to soothe employment and income disruptions.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the Resilience Budget, the Government announced wage support for local employees to cover nine months of wages.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is to be paid to the employers, set at a base support level of 25%, with 50% support for food services and 75% for aviation and tourism-related sectors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: There have been calls for the Government to widen the definitions of qualifying businesses in the various sectors as each sector has an eco-system of suppliers of goods and services that will rise and fall with the industry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: As an example, the industry for Meetings, Incentives, Conventions and Exhibitions (MICE) is listed in the Budget for enhanced wage support at 75% but only for operators of purpose-built MICE venues.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, it was pointed out in a Business Times article on 3 April that contractors who provided MICE-specific products and services to those venues, would only get the 25% base level wage support.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such an anomaly should be reviewed as each industry has a supply chain and eco-system that will be similarly impacted.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: The situation is even more acute with the circuit-breaker policy in place.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: It would also be opportune for the Government to clarify how the JSS will directly benefit workers since the wage offsets are paid to employers rather than to the employees.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Prime Minister Heng has urged employers who receive the JSS to hold on to their workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: However, prior to the Resilience Budget, many employers had already initiated their own cost management schemes by asking employees to take salary cuts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, some airline staff have been asked to go on no-pay leave for varying periods.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: With airlines now getting 75% wage offset from the taxpayer, is there any obligation on employers to review these no-pay leave arrangements reached earlier, to see if they are still justified after the wage offsets?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To take another example, retail shops have had minimal sales and some employers have asked staff to work reduced hours and accept pay cuts.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Over the weekend, after the circuit-breaker policy was announced, employers in non-essential services have told staff that their job situation was not assured.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To be sure, employers without revenue have to make tough choices and I understand that.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To that end, I note that Deputy Prime Minister Heng's speech included a hope that those who receive support will use the resources wisely and responsibly, and that the Government will not hesitate to take action against any abuse.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In the context of the Jobs Support Scheme, could the Minister clarify what would constitute abuse by an employer?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Next, I move on to assisting retrenched and unemployed workers.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To assist retrenched and unemployed workers, the Resilience Budget offers the Temporary Relief Fund and the COVID-19 Support Grant.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: For instance, take an employee of a company which had been incurring losses even before COVID-19 broke.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: If that is the case, it would seem very harsh as it is going to be very difficult for him to find a new job in the current environment.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: I assumed he had been doing such assignments for some time and asked him how it was going.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To my surprise, he said that he had just started with Grab that very day and narrated the turbulence he faced since the start of the year.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In January, he was working as a restaurant manager but, due to poor business, the restaurant had to close.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: He then tried switching to be a mini-bus driver but due to the lack of tourists, he had to abandon that idea.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: To make matters worse, his wife had concurrently lost her job, too, as she worked in the travel industry.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: And to top it off, they have two children aged 14 and 12 to raise.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This family's experience is, unfortunately, becoming more common and affecting more industries.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: This is also a time for reflection and appreciating what we may have taken for granted all this while.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It feels as though we are living in a science fiction film, and not a particularly believable one.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Globally, the first 100,000 cases of COVID took three months to be discovered.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The next 100,000 cases – one month, and then it was one week.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Now, we are adding more than 100,000 cases in a single day.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We are fighting a war, not a conventional war but, nonetheless, a war.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This might be the biggest crisis the world has ever faced in modern times.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It knows no borders nor nationalities nor social classes, none of the traditional lines that divide society.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It also sends a very powerful message of the need to prevent inequality to be a societal fault line.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Rich parents are clamouring for schools to be shut in order to protect their children while poor parents are appealing for schools to be open, because they cannot stay at home.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: They cannot work from home or WFH, as the new acronym goes.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Either way, the Government is holding a very difficult line.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It has to decide to protect lives or to protect livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is truly an unenviable task trying to balance such conflicting goals.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But the role of the Government, especially in a crisis, is to hold the fabric of society together.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Failure to do so will result in voter rebellion.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Occupy Wall Street, Occupy Central, French Revolution; the pitchforks are just one crisis away.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Self-serving behaviour will only make the crisis much more dangerous than it needs to be.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: The neighbour who chooses to go out, not because he needs to but because he wants to, represents a failure of our society to inculcate the right values.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It can fail and it can fail spectacularly.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And, today, it has done so once again.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the challenge is truly existential, only the state can offer a solution that is impactful and equitable for everyone.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: As a buyer of last resort, the state, the Government needs make sure that businesses stay afloat and workers have jobs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When hotels are running at 20% occupancy, the Government can step in and utilise their beds as quarantine facilities.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the store owner is facing bankruptcy, the Government can step in and offer rental rebates and other reliefs.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: When the delivery worker, the gig worker, the restaurant staff cannot make a living by working from home, the Government can step in and offer unemployment benefits.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It needs the strong hand of the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Having a buffer for productive resources in our strategic industries might be inefficient, but it is not a cost.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It is simply the premium we pay for insurance because one day – such as today – when we need to ramp up the productive capacities of our strategic industries, there would be no price too high for us to pay.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, while the case might be strong for us to strengthen our domestic supply chain, we cannot turn out backs on globalisation and free trade.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: This pandemic will change the rules of international engagement.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It will increase nationalism and experts have predicted a retreat from globalisation.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: It will shift power from West to East.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Already, we have seen countries banning the exports of masks, a Singapore student getting beaten up in London, China exercising its soft power by delivering aid to Western countries in a total reversal of roles.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But, paradoxically, this pandemic has also shown that the world is a global village.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We all got sick together and, to overcome this, we all must stick together.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We need to continue to participate in international forums, especially the World Health Organization, because that remains critical for us to find a vaccine in order to defeat the virus.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Singapore must also use this opportunity to enhance our strategic position.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have shown the world that we can lead in many ways.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: We have a high level of trust between the Government and the people.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And we must continue to allow the world to be confident that we can be relevant and contribute to the international society of states.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because all of us know that, if we are not at the table, we are on the table.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Tough choices need to be made and everyone has to make sacrifices in order to preserve our way of life.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But they need to know that these decisions are made based on science and fact, not politics nor personal advantage.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because to solve big problems, we need big trust between the people and the Government.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Not opportunism, not populism, not ideologies, not slogans.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: For the Government to retain the public's trust, it cannot distort facts nor try to manipulate the public with misleading headlines, as we have seen in many countries – so-called "first world countries" – trying to do this and they are suffering the consequences of it.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: But it is not the time to pat ourselves on the back.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Because, like a goalkeeper, who can make 20 great saves but he makes a single error and lets in a single goal and people will suffer.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: And in this case, the price for error of judgement is death.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: So, we got to keep our eyes on the ball and continue to have the courage and conviction to make the right call.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Some nations and their leaders have reacted decisively by recognising the initial signs of danger.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: Others have prevaricated and brought disaster upon their citizens.

speaker: Mr Ong Teng Koon (Marsiling-Yew Tee)
text: To quote my immensely courageous and respected friend and mentor, Mr Lim Swee Say, "Singapore together, Majullah forever".

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The situation in relation to COVID-19 is a rapidly evolving one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: We get daily reports of the numbers of cases being detected, both in Singapore and around the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Even if we take a snapshot of the situation each time we debated this Budget, we see a different world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: When the original Budget Statement was announced in February and debated in March, Singapore had just over 100 cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, at least locally, we looked like we have turned a corner.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the time when I made my speech, there were more people making recoveries and only a small number of additional cases.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, the situation in China appeared to be getting under control.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And at that time, there was the beginning of cases starting in other parts of the world and there were some concerns that we may have a second wave.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Barely a few weeks later, the world had changed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The additional restrictions, already felt serious at that time, included the closing of bars and nightclubs, prohibiting large gatherings of more than 250 people, and many religious gatherings were also called off around that time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Safe distancing measures were also put into place, workplaces were required to implement Business Continuity Plans – all of these were intended to help us carry on with life.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Although the Resilience Budget was only two weeks ago, the latest restrictive measures, the circuit breakers that have been announced, made even those measures seem like indulgent luxuries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, with the latest measures, we will no longer be able to eat out or gather for any reasons outside of work.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only exception to this are those providing essential services.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For the rest of us, the message is clear: stay home as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: That is the best contribution that we can make.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In my own family, my wife, my daughter and I are all going to be at home together for a long time.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: But I think this is the message that we all have to understand and live with.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is going to be a different world for us, but only for one month, if we do things right.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: All these strict controls and measures mean that the social norms will change as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It will no longer be socially acceptable to meet up with friends outside of work and even meeting extended family members is not encouraged.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, what this means is we have to find new ways to connect with people who are close and dear to us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Most Singaporeans fully understand the need for these measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: On Sunday, I walked around to just talk to a few of the hawkers in our area to find out how many of them would be operating.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And most of them said they would continue to operate but probably for shorter hours.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, please, continue to get your daily necessities that you need from them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The markets and supermarkets will remain open, so there is no need for panic buying, but please make fewer trips and just go there to buy what you need and then go back.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the things that I think we all have to be conscious about is that the situation is, indeed, very serious.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Yet, new clusters were found in workers' dormitories.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, there is yet another flank that has opened up.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our contact tracing teams are working incredibly hard.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And while there is community spread, this is not yet widespread.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: So, there is a little bit of pain for all of us to put up with in the month ahead.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And in that respect, I think the Solidarity Budget is welcome.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If things turn the corner, then we may face a better future after that.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If not, especially if people do not take the circuit breaker measures seriously, then we may end up in a much more dire situation and maybe even deeper drawdowns may have to be made.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Like many colleagues, I also dropped by the community centres where the temporary relief schemes were being administered and spoke to the residents there to find out how they were coping, and these were many of the people who have been affected by the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These include Grab and taxi drivers, retail assistants and promoters, workers in the entertainment industry and food and beverage industry.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many, particularly the vulnerable ones who were not on full-time contracts, had their hours or working times reduced.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of the things that struck me was that, under their pain, were resilience and gratitude.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: They understood the measures were necessary and were grateful for the help provided to ride through the storm.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In these times of great crisis, we sometimes see the best in people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: One of our local hawkers in the Admiralty area, Ah Lock, told me he intended to stay open and to provide free meals for needy residents.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was both to help those in need as well as to keep his workers employed.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It is definitely not going to be rosy for him financially, but he feels that this is the right thing to do.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Another person who has actually come out in an extraordinary way was my local provision shop owner in the Vista Point Market.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: This was an initiative that he came up with before COVID-19 and which he carried through.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And it is little efforts like this that show the common humanity in all of us that no matter what we are running through, there is still something we can do for other people.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In many of the efforts that have come forward to distribute masks, volunteers have come forward to help, the hand sanitiser distribution likewise.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And every time we asked for help, people come forward to help.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Now, as we go forward, the next biggest help we need to ask from everyone is to stay at home, look after your health and look after the health of your loved ones.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Budget provides support for many of the most difficult pain points we will face in this coming month.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: And if we all do our part, this will, hopefully, not be too long drawn.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: (In Tamil):   This is probably one of the most difficult challenges we have faced as a country since our Independence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In order to prevent the spread of COVID-19, we have had to take measures that will make many parts of our economy ground to a halt.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those of you working in areas like aviation, tourism, food and beverage or driving Grab or taxis, you will likely have seen your income drop significantly.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: If you have not sought help already, do drop by your Community Centres where the assistance schemes are being administered for those economically impacted by these measures.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Likewise, do let your family and friends who have been affected know as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For those whose businesses may be affected by the crunch in workers, please understand that measures are being taken to keep the workers in dormitories safe as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The next one month will be difficult, both economically and emotionally for all of us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Many of us will feel the economic pinch, either directly or indirectly, as work is disrupted on a large scale.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Our children are going to be at home as well, and many parents will feel the challenge of having to assist with home-based learning for their children while they themselves try to work from home as well.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, we will not be able to visit extended family members who do not live with us.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Indeed, personally, my family will also be going through all of this.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: However, we must understand that if we all do our part and get this right, the pain may be temporary and, after one month, we may be able to ease the restrictions a little.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: For this to work, we must all do our part.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I rise to affirm my support for the recently delivered Singapore Supplementary Budget Statement 2020 and to provide a response from the manufacturing and business community.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The general sentiment from the manufacturing and business community is largely one of relief and pleasant surprise.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: No doubt, our cost of manufacturing here is high.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, it set a precedent for existing businesses and potential MNC investors that, in times of crisis, Singapore Government is willing to stretch its hands and walk through the crisis with us. 感恩政府的借助，关关难过，关关过 ." I believe that after today, he will be very comforted that his trust is really well-placed.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In this regard, following the lead of the Government, as one of the larger local Trade Associations and Chambers (TACs), the SMF will continue to stand united and work with our other TACs and Government agencies to provide assistance for our businesses through the current challenging times.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Only three months have passed from the first confirmed COVID-19 case in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, it probably feels way longer than that to most Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The way of life, as many knew before, has been disrupted.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: For example, we see more alcohol everywhere today than rice available for sale in supermarkets.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The former, of course, in hand sanitisers and, the latter, due to the irrational panic buying sentiments of some.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Unprecedented in both scale and depth, this second round or third round of stimulus measures demonstrates a calculated, prudent and progressive approach by the Government to address the wide-ranging effects of the COVID-19 outbreak which is widespread globally.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Apart from the targeted support to the different industries most directly affected by the current global pandemic, the Supplementary Budget sets out broad-based support for businesses and reflects an understanding by the Government of the difficulties that companies are facing on the ground.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The 3Cs of cost, cash and credit, indeed, represent the most immediate challenges many businesses face.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As a TAC, we are committed to helping our members gain access to this support framework.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: However, in fulfilling this role of "connector", I have received some feedback which I hope the Government can take into consideration.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: There are some additional measures in today's Solidarity Budget.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: So, can the Government please consider reducing or waiving the cost of such, during these times so as to allow for even more manoeuvrability for our SMEs during the difficult times ahead?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Can such firms also be given some assistance in the form of road tax relief or even diesel tax relief from the reduced use of such vehicles in these difficult times?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: I take and share the unwavering stand that the support rendered in the Supplementary Budget cannot be taken for granted, and businesses cannot just sit around and wait for Government assistance.
