text: We must be prepared to extend help to all Singaporeans and we must give that help before our fellow Singaporeans even realise that they need the help.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: The MUBI scheme is also financed on the principle of solidarity, because all Singaporeans must face the COVID-19 pandemic together.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Therefore, all Singaporean taxpayers are asked to contribute towards financing the scheme.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: Some will give more, but all will give some.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I fully support those measures and the hard work that went intof them.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: If the damage caused by COVID-19 persists we must do more.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: In this spirit, we propose the MUBI scheme.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: From the Unity, to Resilience, to Solidarity Budgets, it is clear that the Government is listening hard and responding with great competence, boldness and heart.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The resources needed to fight this escalating crisis seem unending.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: More than 3.9 billion people or half the world's population have been asked to remain in their homes to combat COVID-19.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: After battling the virus for over two months, with successive restrictions, Singapore too, joined those confined to their homes, in an effort to slow the worrying growth rate of unlinked local cases.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I fully support these enhanced new measures, designed to be circuit breaker to arrest the escalating infections, such restrictions will incur significant economic costs in addition to imposing a severely constrained way of living on everyone.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: No one is sure how widely the COVID-19 pandemic will spread and when it will peak.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Containment may take longer than currently projected and no country has seen a clear path to recovery.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Even China, which has seen its reported infections dwindle, has urged their citizens to avoid non-essential outings and has continued to discourage foreigners from entering, in order to prevent a resurgence of infections.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Without widespread availability of a viable vaccine, the removal of restrictions on economic activity is likely to be painfully slow.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The longer the duration of lock-down, the more complicated the resumption of economic activity will be.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Would he extend a similar set of support measures?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: It is at times like this when we feel grateful of the privileged financial position Singapore is in, endowed as it is with the wherewithal to weather this storm.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Our reserves have enabled Deputy Prime Minister to act decisively when the nation faces such extraordinary circumstances.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The lion share of Resilience and Solidarity Budgets will go towards the Job Support Scheme in order to save jobs and protect people's livelihoods.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I am pleased that the Government chose to bear the full costs of savings jobs with wage support, instead of cutting CPF.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: After the previous CPF rate cut in 2003, it took eight years for the employer contribution rate to be restored to 16%.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I hope we can continue to safeguard CPF for our workers in this crisis.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Despite the strong efforts on Job Support Scheme, less than half of the Singaporeans polled by The Straits Times believe that the measures would be enough to rescue jobs.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: There is no historical precedent of the type of economic dislocations that we are experiencing.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: More are drawing parallels with the trauma wrought by World War II or the Great Depression.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I note that some countries, such as Australia, eligibility for wage support only kicks in if business turnover drops by 30% due to the pandemic – so there is an eligibility criteria.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: And for larger companies with turnover of more than A$1 billion, their drop in turnover must be at least 50% before they are eligible.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Whilst I agree with the broad-based approach Singapore is taking, it is incumbent on companies who enjoy disproportionately greater benefits to “do the right thing”, and share these benefits with their business partners, employees and the wider eco-system, in the spirit of solidarity.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Food delivery platforms such as Grab and Deliveroo typically charge 30%-35% in commission fees.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: This means food outlets need to pay an exorbitant one-third of customer receipts, in fees to delivery platforms, as commissions for delivery.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Judging by the compensation that delivery platforms pay their riders and charges they impose on consumers for delivery, I think this seems excessive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Owners of food outlets have told me that the high commissions are barely tolerable during "peacetime".

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: However, with the onset of COVID-19, deliveries have now become the dominant portion of their business – indeed, the only mode of business from today, for at least a month.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Under these circumstances, payment of such commissions renders the sustainability of food establishments untenable.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I urge, and I really urge, GrabFood, Food Panda and Deliveroo to do their part – review their commission model and foster more equitable sharing of costs and benefits with food outlets owners, riders and consumers.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: I believe it is in the delivery companies’ interests to adjust their commission rates, so that food outlets may have a fighting chance to survive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As for delivery riders who "brave" the deliveries to ferry our favourites to us at home, we as consumers can also play our part by giving them a little extra.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Should those of us who can afford it not consider tipping our delivery riders 5%-10% of food receipts as a discretionary "service fee"?

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: We can all do our part to keep Singapore’s treasured, unique and colourful food culture alive.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In the coming days, more relationships between parties will need to evolve and creative new models that benefit all stakeholders must emerge.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Many of our PRs are part of Singaporean families and have contributed socially and economically.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: In solidarity, could the Deputy Prime Minister consider giving them some help, even if not the full $600, means tested on a case by case basis, and applicants can be asked to show that they are part of Singaporean families.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Also there are many Long-Term Visit Pass holders who are spouses of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: They would certainly appreciate this, even if it is just a fraction of $600.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: The Unity, Resilience and Solidarity Budgets provide comprehensive measures for individuals and companies to build capabilities for the eventual recovery at all levels.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Despite our best efforts, some companies and jobs will disappear, but new ones will emerge.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Those who stay resilient in the face of hardship and adversity will be rewarded, when a new dawn breaks.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: As we face the mighty storm together, for days, months or even years, our shared sense of identity and solidarity will be our greatest strength.

speaker: Ms Foo Mee Har (West Coast)
text: Every generation of Singaporeans has been defined by its own crisis; each has come through stronger and more united than before – this challenge is ours to face down, as one united people.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Arts and sporting events, and CCAs, were cancelled or postponed even before the new circuit breaker measures that take effect today, 7 April.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To deal with this unprecedented crisis, the government has introduced additional measures to protect livelihoods, help businesses overcome immediate challenges and strengthen economic and social resilience.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We will: (a) protect livelihoods and careers in the arts, culture and sports eco-systems; (b) invest in capabilities that will position ourselves well for the post-COVID recovery; and (c) digitalise these sectors to create new markets, provide new job opportunities and ensure that Singaporeans can continue to benefit from the arts, culture and sports.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We must first protect the livelihoods of our arts, culture and sports practitioners.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Individual professionals, such as freelancers, may tap on broad-based relief schemes like the Temporary Relief Fund and SEP Income Relief Scheme or SIRS, and defer their income tax payments and mortgage instalments.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will support all eligible companies and employees in the arts and culture and sports sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MCCY will announce additional support for major companies, as well as leading arts and culture groups, shortly at a later date.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To help companies and businesses further defray costs, all eligible tenants in MCCY-owned properties – be they in the arts and culture, youth, or sports – will benefit from the two months of rental waiver announced by the Deputy Prime Minister.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These measures will provide some immediate relief for our arts and culture companies and allow them to use this period – when they are working from home – to plan for the future with greater assurance and certainty.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While many of these jobs will not be available while circuit breaker measures are in place, we are preparing them now so that we can start hiring as soon as these measures are relaxed.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Beyond relief support, we will invest in retaining and upskilling the arts, culture and sports professionals.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We want to protect and sustain the breadth and depth of skillsets and talents in the eco-systems as much as possible.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Practitioners in these sectors will already benefit from the $500 to $1,000 SkillsFuture Credit top-up, and the SEP Training Support Scheme.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I encourage our practitioners to hone their professional skills, and explore new complementary skills through the many online courses that are available from home.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For the sports sector, we have been working with partners to build up the range of Continuing Coach Education or CCE courses to upskill our coaches and instructors.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: When the situation allows, coaches and instructors can avail themselves of more than 3,000 training opportunities by end-2020.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is in addition to the more than 2,000 ActiveSG SkillsFuture training opportunities currently available to coaches and instructors.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These courses are either free or well covered by training grants from SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Arts and culture freelancers, as well as those in the wider creative sector who provide important complementary expertise such as sound and lighting professionals, hold essential capabilities for our arts and culture eco-system.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Arts Resource Hub or ARH under the National Arts Council or NAC, has been set up to promote employability and sustainability of freelancers’ careers by providing resources and services.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The ARH has been engaging and surveying a wide range of cultural and creative freelancers over the past months to better understand their profiles and the impact of COVID-19 on them.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It helps us refine our range of shared resources and services, and provide reliable and relevant information to help them tide over this difficult period.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Freelancers who have experienced contract cancellations can also seek advice from the ARH.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I strongly encourage all cultural and creative freelancers to sign up online with the ARH, at no cost, to enjoy the convenience of a centralised point-of-contact.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This is the time for companies to invest in their employees.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Enhanced Training Support scheme announced by the Deputy Prime Minister provides absentee payroll to employers who send their employees for training in SkillsFuture courses and is open to companies in the arts, culture and sports sectors.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: In addition, arts and culture organisations can apply for further support under the expanded Capability Development Scheme for the Arts or CDSA administered by NAC, to send their employees for professional-led training courses, beyond those endorsed by SkillsFuture.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Up to 200 companies will benefit from this.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These freelancers can apply for the CDSA to participate in a variety of courses, including local and international online courses.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These include masterclasses in graphic communication skills in outreach with digital media, courses in creative writing, music production and studio recording.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC will invite suggestions on training programmes and welcome courses by our own major arts companies and established professionals who are keen to offer their skills and experience in their areas of expertise.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Just like companies and their employees, freelancers can also use this time to apply for the CDSA and use it to take online courses, or for future training.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Arts, culture and sports lift our spirits in these difficult times, and sustain our emotional and physical well-being.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: To ensure Singaporeans continue to have access to the arts, culture and sports during the next few months, our culture and sports agencies will be releasing digital content to engage Singaporeans even as we stay at home, provide enjoyment for the entire family, and encourage them to keep fit.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Interested audiences can view available offerings at NAC’s A-List website, an integrated platform featuring cultural offerings from our cultural institutions, arts groups and artists to offer greater access and connectivity for audiences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: A-List is already available with many exciting programmes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We also want to step up on-going digitalisation efforts to enhance capabilities of the arts and culture, and sports sector, create new experiences for audiences and participants, and expand economic opportunities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Beyond bringing their products online, we see that it is a good time for the sector to acquire technical skills in data analytics, audience sensing, online marketing and more.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: For the arts and culture sector, we have established a Digitalisation Fund to support arts and culture groups and practitioners, cultural institutions, and cultural festival organisers to go digital with their arts and culture content.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will be open to all arts and culture groups and practitioners, including freelancers.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Artists and arts groups offering student-facing programmes including NAC Arts Education Programme (AEP) providers are encouraged to apply to NAC for this support to create digital content that can be offered for online use by schools.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: While some ideas may only be possible to execute after the circuit breaker measures, I encourage arts and culture groups and practitioners to prepare and submit their grant proposals now, so that they can bring their best work to Singaporeans once the situation improves.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC also welcomes proposals which include creative means to develop digital projects while fully working from home.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Digitalisation Fund will support large-scale digitalisation of existing festivals and projects.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are committed to continuing with our annual large-scale festivals through digital means.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: As far as possible, we will hold digital editions of Singapore Heritage Festival in June, Singapore Writers Festival and Arts in Your Neighbourhood in November, followed by Singapore Art Week in January 2021.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They will involve virtual arts and culture presentations, workshops, and tours.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NAC and Arts House Limited will work with local arts groups involved in the Singapore International Festival of the Arts 2020 to explore how they can offer innovative arts and culture experiences digitally later in the year.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Digitalisation Fund will also support the digitalisation of our museum exhibitions and collections.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The National Heritage Board (NHB) will progressively make available virtual exhibitions of the galleries at our national museums and heritage institutions, so that Singaporeans and international visitors alike can experience and learn about heritage without leaving their homes.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: NHB will also be working with Museum Roundtable members to support similar projects, and assist them in building up their digitalisation capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: SportSG will leverage technology to continue to engage Singaporeans in sports events and activities in this period.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: It will set up the ActiveSG Circle, a virtual sports centre in the form of an online platform.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will enable citizens to stay connected and active with an expansive offering, a wide offering of content such as exercise videos, programmes, talks, workshops and even races through a virtual space.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: This will benefit all eligible companies and employees in the arts, culture and sports, sector.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: MCCY will also provide additional support for major companies, as well as leading arts and culture groups.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: More details will be announced at a later date.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Also, we want to quicken the pace of digitalisation efforts of the arts and cultural sector via the new Digitalisation Fund.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The Arts Resource Hub (ARH) under NAC will continue to promote sustainability of freelancers' careers by providing shared resources and services, including advising them on various support schemes by the government, to tide them over this difficult period.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: (In English): Mr Speaker, if I may summarise.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: The relief packages announced by Deputy Prime Minister provide financial support to the individuals affected, sustain the eco-systems of these sectors by minimising the loss of capabilities, and raise the capabilities of the sectors in the physical and digital spaces.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Individuals can benefit from financial reliefs, such as the Temporary Relief Fund, SIRS for freelancers and the COVID-19 Support Grant; training subsidies and grants in the Capability Development Scheme for the Arts to build their long-term capabilities.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: They will also benefit from the temporary jobs SportSG will be making available.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Companies can benefit from wage support measures such as the enhanced JSS, and the Enhanced Training Support scheme and the CDSA.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our push to digitalise these sectors will provide economic opportunities to both individuals and companies, and allow them to continue bringing arts and sports experiences to Singaporeans.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: These schemes will be relevant even when circuit breaker measures are applicable, and will help us emerge stronger.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Everyone has a part to play to overcome the situation we face.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: We are in this together, and the arts, culture, and sports communities must work together, work with the public, to protect the safety of our patrons, students and audiences.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I urge larger and more established groups with deeper capabilities to help the smaller ones and individual practitioners, and ask that corporations, foundations and members of the public continue supporting the arts and culture and sports.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: All of us should take this time to prepare, with agility and resourcefulness, to welcome our audiences and students again with better creations, better works, greater competencies and broader outreach.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: Our arts, culture and sports sectors have proven their resilience time and again.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: I am confident that they will be ready with our best shows, most creative content, and highest quality classes once Singapore is ready for us, so that arts, culture and sports will be an even more important part of people’s lives.

speaker: The Minister for Culture, Community and Youth (Ms Grace Fu Hai Yien)
text: COVID-19 is a test and we will rise to the occasion.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The COVID-19 pandemic, with the effects of lockdown or stay-at-home orders, has brought a standstill to businesses all over the world and Singapore has not been spared, too.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond aviation, tourism and F&B, most industries and sectors in Singapore have been affected, some earlier than others.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The effect on economies worldwide will be an unprecedented one, possibly worse than any global economic downturns we have ever seen since the Great Depression.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The economic fall-outs may go on for quite a while after the COVID-19 pandemic has been tamed.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I declare my interest as an SME owner.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the businesses of our SMEs are affected, many Singaporeans they employ are in turn affected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While the aviation, tourism and F&B sectors may be badly affected, the vast majority of our SMEs outside of the aviation, tourism and F&B sectors lament they will get much less than the 75% or 50% wage support received by the priority sectors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Who is to say that businesses in other sectors are not as badly affected or will not be as badly affected?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Since the Resilience Budget has been proposed on 26 March, has any study been done to assess the grave effect the pandemic has or is about to have on all business sectors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On 24 March 2020, the Government announced that all centre-based tuition and enrichment centres will be suspended.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The reason given is the need to reduce the intermingling of students from different schools and enhance the safety of our students.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This brings to a stop the daily bustling activities that take place in our tuition and enrichment centres during both weekdays and weekends.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: While some of the tuition centres may have resorted to online learning, yet online learning has not been able to completely replace many of the pre-existing programmes in the tuition centres and enrichment centres.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some programmes may not be suitable for online learning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some tutors, are for various reasons, not able to convert their face-to-face programmes to online modules.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some parents are also, for various reasons, not keen to convert existing programmes to online learning or even via Zoom, when offered.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many parents prefer traditional methods of personal teaching.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Habits and mindsets will always take time to change, but that is scant comfort to businesses suffering the sudden shock to their businesses brought about by the abrupt ban.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For centres who may not have locked in their students' subscriptions for a longer time, having chosen to collect fees on a monthly basis, they face abrupt loss of revenue as some parents have not continued to pay the fees.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Learning service providers to MOE schools and to pre-schools are another group of SMEs in the education industry which have been affected from an even earlier time, with all outdoor programmes and all large-attendance programmes being cancelled in early February and co-curricular activities (CCAs) in March.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Given the requirements in pre-schools that trainers cannot teach in other schools concurrently and students of different classes cannot share the same enrichment classes, many enrichment classes had to be cancelled from February onwards, with many left without any revenue.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Besides a significant loss in revenue, these SME businesses still face the pressures of premise rental and staff salary.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government's offer to pay 25% of the salary of their staff up to the first $4,600 under the JSS – which is just a few percentage points above the amount of employer's CPF contributions the employers will have to pay for each staff per month anyway – may assist to a certain extent, but it may not be significant enough to save jobs – the reason stated by Deputy Prime Minister Heng for the Resilience Budget.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How will the Government provide greater assistance to these businesses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: At this point, let me touch on one further aspect of the Jobs Support Scheme or JSS, again.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I understand that in the private education business, there are many people in such a position – sole proprietors, partners or company shareholders of their businesses – who are at the same time registered employees of their business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those such persons can be regarded as self-employed in some ways.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I believe that this situation is not unique to the private education business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There are many in our micro-SMEs in other industries or sectors who are in the same situation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On Sunday, I met one of our residents, who runs a phone repair business and who is in this exact position.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: How would the Government help these affected Singaporeans?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For parents who send their children to MOE Kindergartens and pre-schools run by anchor and partner operators, including those run by PAP Community Foundation (PCF) and NTUC, they are already entitled to various subsidies.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But for other SME operators, where Singaporean parents only get the standard subsidies, or for faith-based kindergartens, where there are zero subsidies, the net refund that these operators must cough up is relatively much higher as the net fees payable are higher compared to MOE Kindergartens and those run by anchor and partner operators.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Furthermore, many operators had to incur extra costs recently to have additional manpower to cover for those on Leave of Absence (LOA) or five-day medical leave, and for extra cleaning works.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I have dealt in some detail on the private education industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: However, it is but one example out of many businesses which have been affected by the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the circuit breaker announcements, things will get worse for many businesses in the coming month or longer, especially the many businesses that do not thrive on working remotely.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The property tax rebate, together with the savings by way of the rental rebate, will be helpful in some ways to alleviate the sharp pain, and so will the Jobs Support Scheme.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But will it be enough to ensure the survival of the business and to save jobs?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Just last week, one of our residents, who is a chartered accountant in his 30s, shared with me that he has just been retrenched from a mid-sized accounting firm and is struggling to find employment in his industry.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Indeed, if business is down, businesses will struggle to pay all their business expenses until a certain level of business has resumed – especially many SMEs, who may have precious little to sustain their business expenses, including rent and income beyond a few months.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This economic crisis is likely to hang over the world for quite some time.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Beyond the Resilience and Solidarity Budgets, how will the Government assist businesses and Singaporeans to stay afloat in the coming months and beyond?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I move away from businesses, I would like to seek some clarifications regarding arts businesses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: With the cancellation of entertainment, our flourishing arts professionals have to cancel their plays, musicals, concerts and other performances, and shows, which may go on until the end of the year.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When performances are cancelled, there are no ticket sales and corporate sponsorships are often cancelled – not to mention that in these difficult times, it is challenging to expect support from many corporate sponsors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Many of these arts businesses are registered charities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If not, what is the corresponding assistance being given to this group of arts businesses?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In MOM's paper titled "Labour Force in Singapore 2019", it was mentioned that in the year ending June 2019, and I quote from paragraph 1.1.9, "211,000 residents were engaged in own account work as some form of employment" and own account workers were defined in the same paper as, and I quote from paragraph 1.17, "individuals who operate their own business or trade without employing any paid employees".

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In principle, the concern with setting a figure – a limit – at all, on this is that we are talking about a special economic crisis situation caused by the global COVID-19 pandemic, which has developed suddenly.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: These self-employed people see their livelihoods being adversely affected in a short time and require quick and immediate assistance from the Government, regardless the nature of their residences.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The property that they live in or own or co-own may not be relevant to their current income and earning capacity as well as most relevantly, their present position of suffering from sudden financial problems due to the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they own such property, is the Government expecting such self-employed people to sell their property quickly?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If so, is it really fair or realistic to expect such persons to sell their homes immediately in such a market condition?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is different from the usual situation of people applying for financial assistance due to longer term employment and so on.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I move on to help for our taxi and private hire drivers.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is already a well-known fact that our taxi drivers and private hire drivers are suffering from a huge drop in business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A resident who has a private car hire licence and serves his own source of customers had checked and was told that he did not qualify.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If it is true, may I know the rationale behind this?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I urge the Government to look into this.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I look forward to the Government rendering more assistance to more of our affected Singaporeans and SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I will not talk about opportunities this time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The focus should be on getting through this to the other side – a post-COVID world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Other things should not distract Singaporeans from this mission right now.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Before I begin, I declare my interest as a CEO and a shareholder in a company providing research and consulting.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I would argue that what we should fight is not fear.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Rather, we should fight the twin evils of indifference, complacency and unscientific views, on the one hand, and unbridled panic, on the other.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A little fear may actually be helpful, keeping us on our toes and mitigating the risk that bad habits will return at the first sign of good news.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But it should be a little fear for everyone and not only a little fear for ourselves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: That should come from trust in the scientific view that if most people get sick, no one will be safe as individuals and families.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: As the famous scientist, Neil deGrasse Tyson, recently said, this COVID-19 crisis will put to the test a key question: does society listen to scientists?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We all have a role to play in answering that question as a country.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: All of us react differently to an event like this based on our personalities, medical profiles, socio-economic circumstances and many things besides.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is easier for some of us to work from home than others, for example.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Recognising these differences means accepting that there will be questions, there will be discussions, there will be debate, trade-offs and, yes, course correction.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is unity that will ultimately breed success in this effort but it is understanding that will beget unity.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is openness and accountability that will get us to understanding and it is our democratic society enshrined in our pledge that will beget openness and accountability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: On social media, there are many chat threads openly saying that authoritarianism has worked, democracy has failed.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Look at China versus Italy and the USA.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet some of the countries that have done well through this crisis thus far, like Taiwan, South Korea and Japan, have open democratic systems.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We would do well not to draw the wrong conclusions about democracy as many who lived through the Great Depression of the 1930s did, with disastrous results for the world.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: This is what the reserves principal has been saved to do.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Workers' Party supports the idea of not touching the reserves principal except in times of crisis, as I said in Parliament last month.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, I will speak about a few issues and potential gaps.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: First, Sir, on the most vulnerable in our society.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those who are homeless I know that wonderful not-for-profit organisations (NPOs) like Homeless Hearts of Singapore, New Home Community Services and many others are stepping efforts to help this vulnerable group.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What are the outreach efforts being put in place by MSF and other arms of the Government?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And what support has been given to NPOs to ensure that these extremely vulnerable people can access medical and economic support at this time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Over the past four years has been my privilege to work with our volunteers to deliver assistance of various kinds to those living in rental flats in Serangoon and Bedok.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some of our beneficiary families have done all right.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Two of our beneficiary families recently had children who qualified for entry to an Autonomous University.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I cannot tell you how gladdened I was and how that cheered our volunteers.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Yet, others are not doing so well, and face multiple issues that hinder them and their children in the pursuit of flourishing life.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: For those on ComCare awarded for a period of a few months, renewals are often an extremely stressful experience.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Government has said that their eligibility for ComCare will be eased during COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: My Parliamentary colleague Mr Faisal Manap has also spoken on this issue and made a few suggestions, with which I agree.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now would be the time to be pragmatic and not ideological about such questions.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: We need to get by until the economy comes back with pent-up demand.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: During this time, we should do everything practicable to keep viable SMEs and micro-businesses alive.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If they are wound up, those entrepreneurs may not return, hurting employment and long-term economic growth potentially which needs entrepreneurship to balance other sources of innovation and investment.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The Supplementary Budget has a host of measures for government risk-sharing in loans to SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if the loans do not get to our SMEs, in spite of risk-sharing.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: What if our banks simply do not lend.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our business eco-system does not have the deep historic ties between regional banks and SMEs seen in countries like Japan, Germany and Switzerland that are useful at times like this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Would the Government consider a scheme like what has been introduced in the UK – the Term Funding Scheme – under which participating banks that lend to SMEs get to access lower wholesale funding costs from the central bank.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, banks could still choose not to lend but at least this would tilt the balance towards our SMEs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, many SMEs do not want to take on loans due to pessimism about their ability to repay after the crisis.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And this is where job support and rental deferment play a role in preventing businesses from closing down, perhaps never to return.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Extended deferment could be made conditional on the company paying back at state, if and when it returns to decent sustained profitability.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Reusable masks are to be self-collected at RCs and CCs.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Anecdotal and social media feedback suggests that some people are reluctant to collect these masks for various reasons including inertia and fears about potential exposure.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Some wonder why self-collection was used when all are told to stay at home unless absolutely necessary.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: When I asked Minister Lawrence Wong about this in the context of distributing surgical masks in February, he said self-collection was used to minimise wastage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our healthcare professionals do not need reusable masks, or do not need them as much as they need surgical masks; and hence, one assumes there are fewer pressures on that stock.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, not that many masks are needed per household since they are reusable.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Those who click on an online site or an app using SingPass, for example, or calling a hotline.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, Mr Speaker, Sir, I should focus about the lessons we can learn from this crisis to better prepare for the next one, whenever that may happen.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Governments around the world are asking companies to shift R&D and production resources to make masks and ventilators.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Even if legal powers are not deployed, is the government using its powers of persuasion and purchase to nudge domestic manufacturers to produce more of such critically needed items which may raise healthcare system capacity and scalability?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Now might be a good time to test our ability to get such things done for when the next crisis hits.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Of course, there are companies that are voluntarily doing this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is commendable of these firms to be doing so.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, there is also news of other countries calling back retired healthcare professionals to serve, to address the kinds of potential manpower shortages that Minister Gan spoke about in February.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Next, what long-term lessons can we draw in dealing with future pandemics?

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: A letter appeared in The Straits Times Forum on 28 March.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The full letter is available online; and I quote "The reason why robust fiscal measures such as the Resilience Budget are possible is due to financial discipline and prudence and growing Singapore's reserves at a the strong rate all this time.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Had we for whatever reasons rested on our laurels and grown our reserves at a slower rate as was suggested before and" and in brackets, it says "grow reserves at a slower rate to invest in Singaporeans, Leon Perera, 28 February". "The Resilience Budget would not be possible and we would now be in economic dire straits due to the COVID-19 pandemic." I sent a reply to this letter on the same day, which The Straits Times Forum has not published to the best of my knowledge.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Please allow me to read out a part of that reply. "In 2008, the Government introduced the Net Investment Returns Framework where half of the long-term expected real returns on relevant reserves asset classes can be used for Budget spending.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In 2015, Temasek was added to this framework.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Both of these changes effectively slowed down the reserves growth rate, but surely few of us today would argue that these changes were irresponsible because they slowed reserves growth.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The funds released have been put to constructive use in the Budget.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Our reserves have been estimated at over a trillion dollars.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: The best policies to govern reserves growth versus releasing more Budget funds should thus be different today from what they were in the past.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: To use an analogy from the business world, a start-up company may need to conserve cash to manage cash flow.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: But when it has grown to the point where there is tens of billions in cash, corporate leaders should think about how the cash should be invested for better long-term growth and to benefit stakeholders rather than growing the cash pile at the same rate as when the company was at the start-up stage.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In fact, the Government introducing the current resource framework in 2008, and adding Temasek in 2015, implicitly recognised this point.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There can be over saving just as there can be under saving.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Moreover, releasing more Budget funds can mean investing more in our people and our companies in ways that if successful would enhance the long-term potential growth rate of GDP, productivity and innovation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: If this happens, tax revenue would rise in tandem with GDP thus reducing the need to draw on the reserves and reserves returns.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Singaporeans should have fact-based rational conversations on the right rate of reserves growth versus releasing more Budget funds.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: Such conversations need to address deep strategic and philosophic questions, like what the additional funds could be invested to do, balanced against what possible future emergencies could necessitate drawing down a massive percentage of those reserves.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: It is time to recognise that there can be reasonable viewpoints on both sides of this question.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And in relation to the letter writer's last point, what we will have as a nation to weather the storm the next time a crisis hits, is not only our reserves but more importantly, the solidarity, the resolve and the ingenuity of our people." And this is where I end the quote from that reply and I believe Assoc Prof Theseira actually made a similar point on the last point that I just mentioned.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: I am sharing this now because to me such debate and disagreement is really how we get to real unity and real consensus formation.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: In noting this, I do not blame anyone.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: There is no playbook for a crisis like this.

speaker: Mr Leon Perera (Non-Constituency Member)
text: And if we can get to that we would be one United people who have built a democratic society and one built to last.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many residents have shared how appreciative they are and thanked the Government for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My first point is about those on unpaid leave and reduced working hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The Resilience and Solidarity Budget provides much support to Singaporeans who have lost their jobs and for the self-employed.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: But we need to do more for those who remain in employment but have nonetheless taken a big hit in their incomes.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Such workers can either be workers forced to take pay cuts or go on unpaid leave, or hourly workers who have lost shifts and hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I recently received an email from my resident, whose employer cut her hours from full-time to part-time.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Another resident has been put on unpaid leave for at least three months.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These are not isolated cases and I am sure all Members in this House have received similar calls for help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can the Government provide more financial support for those who have lost income but remain in employment?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is especially important for those put on unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: After all, those on unpaid leave essentially become unemployed for the months they are on unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The reply might be that we are helping employers retain workers through the Jobs Support Scheme but to save at least 25% of salary costs, there might still be employers who will prefer to put workers on unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should provide some level of wage stability for those lucky enough to find themselves still employed but with zero or significantly reduced income.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Parents working in essential services and key economic sectors perform a duty for our nation as they continue going into their workplaces in this time of global pandemic.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, there is a big, unanswered question of what happens when the children of these parents are required to stay at home due to COVID-related health symptoms, school closures, Leaves of Absences or Stay-Home Notices.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: These parents do not have the option to work from home, yet they may have a young child at home during working hours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Some will be lucky enough to have alternative care-giving and caring employers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We should remember that the legal entitlement of childcare leave is already insufficient during a regular year.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As I mentioned in my speech on the Budget debate, parents exhaust it during mandatory pre-school closures and during their children's sickness.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Now, in this most irregular year, school closures and stay-home requirements last for weeks.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: How can they possibly have enough childcare leave to take?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The only option left for them is unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many parents have told me this is indeed what they are taking, but in this business climate, they worry they will lose their jobs if they take too much unpaid leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: There are currently no protections for them, and we need to bear in mind that many have no alternatives and do not have the money to hire additional help.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They desperately need this COVID-related childcare leave so they can keep their jobs and be there for their children.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: In this difficult time, the Government has to step in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My third point is a short and simple one.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: As part of our Care and Support Package, we are giving $300 in cash to every adult Singaporean who has a Singaporean child aged 20 years old and below.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many single unwed parents have written to me asking if they qualify for this.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I think we can all agree that these dark days are not a time for discrimination, and all parents deserve the care and support regardless of their marital status.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Single unwed parents are in an especially tight spot.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They do not have an additional pair of helping hands.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Also, because the median income of single unwed mothers under 35 years old was already $600, they will lack job security and are likely to face losses in wages.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: They, and many other Singaporeans, will also benefit from all the other measures I mentioned before: more financial support for those on unpaid leave and reduced working hours, increased telecommuting and a COVID-related childcare leave.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My final point is about our migrant friends, workers who have left their homes to come and build and clean ours.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: News has emerged that two migrant worker dormitories, S11 @ Punggol and Westlite in Toh Guan have been gazetted as isolation areas.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Many Singaporeans have contacted me to share their concerns for the safety and well-being of these workers.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I must first thank Minister Josephine Teo for her comprehensive Facebook post on the measures taken to prevent transmissions and to ensure that the basic needs of migrant workers are met including food, necessities, salary and medical care.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Migrant worker dormitories are very densely packed and the workers live in very close proximity.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand that measures have been taken to implement safe distancing measures and to thin out the dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: However, even with these measures, the risk of transmission is very high.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: The issue is the conditions the workers live in.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: We have to do more, much more to improve the current living conditions.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This is vital to stop the outbreak in these dormitories.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Beyond the measure we are taking now, I also sincerely hope MOM will do a complete review and ensure that our migrant workers' living conditions are improved significantly.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I am glad Minister Josephine agrees with this and has given her word that action will be taken.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Next, many workers are also afraid that they have been infected with COVID-19.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: To supplement the measures already taken, can we consider proactively testing the workers in dormitories with infected workers, starting with those who lived in closer proximity to the infected workers?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would assist in definitively identifying those infected and quickly isolating them to prevent a further outbreak.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I understand there are limitations for doing this nationwide.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Can we do more extensive testing on a limited scale for this high-risk population?

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This would help to keep Singaporeans safe too and help calm the workers who are extremely worried.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Lastly, as with Singaporeans, the workers are also worried about their livelihoods.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This has provided a lot of assurance to the workers and they are very thankful.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: I hope MOM will follow up and ensure that every worker is paid.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: This will help employers pay and take care of the upkeep of their workers, and prepare their workforce to restart when the circuit breaker is lifted.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: My speech was actually much longer, but a lot of the points I was going to raise were addressed by the Government in the announcements made last week and yesterday.

speaker: Mr Louis Ng Kok Kwang (Nee Soon)
text: Let us make sure that everyone make it through this crisis together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Indeed, we will do all we can to preserve jobs and businesses, and support our workforce.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Last Friday, Prime Minister Lee Hsien Loong announced stringent measures to curb the spread of COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: This is to minimise physical interactions and break the circuit of virus transmission.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Despite the closure, firms that can continue operations with their workers on telecommuting arrangements, should continue to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We understand that companies that had implemented FWAs and telecommuting prior to the enhanced measures, in fact, prior to the COVID-19 crisis, for their staff were better able to operationalise business continuity plans (BCP) quickly.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Half of Singtel's 12,000 employees are already been working from home prior to today.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The majority of them are used to working offsite and they have the infrastructure to do so.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Those who need to be at their workplaces work on staggered work times and also staggered lunch periods.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Some employees start work as early as 7.00 am because that suits them and some as late as 10.00 am.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Of course, those working at 7.00 am, they get to go back home earlier.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: The company's operations continue to run as seamlessly as possible and customers are well-supported.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Another example is legal services firm Allen & Gledhill.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Their lawyers and staff work from home with the support of a robust and secure IT infrastructure that allows them to meet and collaborate remotely.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Ms Jessica Tan, in her many speeches advocated that, it is possible to meet and collaborate with colleagues even as we telecommute or work from home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Chairman and Senior Partner of Allen & Gledhill said this, Ms Christina Ong said, and I quote: "Our focus on embracing technology has meant that when we had to, we could.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: For certain types of work, some of our lawyers now even say that they accomplish even more from home.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: As we move into a period of stricter social distancing, we will make it easier for employers to get support in implementing telecommuting and staggered hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We strongly encourage more companies to apply for the WLG which can be used for the purchase of laptops, software and related equipment for telecommuting.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the immediate term, adopting FWAs will help companies overcome the present challenges posed by COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the long run, FWAs will help companies ride the wave of changing workplace norms, become a more inclusive, caring, and also attractive employer and thereby attracting better talent.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: FWAs have helped companies like Cycle and Carriage become a choice employer, as their staff appreciate the extra time they have with their family, the ability to attend to personal matters and greater flexibility in childcare arrangements.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In Mandarin):   Mr Speaker, Sir, our enterprises are currently already benefiting from MOM's Work-Life Grant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Employers are able to receive $2,000 for every worker on a flexible work arrangement.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Because of the effects of COVID-19, especially during this circuit breaker period, we want to observe safe distancing, so, we need people to work at home or we have staggered working hours.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Therefore, in order to help our employers to provide such flexible working arrangements so that more people will be able to work from home, MOM will make it easier for employers to benefit from this grant.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: At the moment, enterprises have to certify that they have been having this arrangement for six months before they can apply.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Now, we have shortened this period to one month.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In other words, the application criteria have been shortened from six months to one month.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, these relaxed arrangements will apply after the circuit breaker period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will open for application from 20 April 2020 and we encourage companies to apply for the Work-Life Grant which provides flexibility for example, using devices such as portable computers and so on.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the short run , the Work-Life Grant can help companies overcome the challenges brought by COVID-19.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: In the long run, successfully implementing flexible work arrangements will not only help our companies to keep on improving productivity, it would actually help them become more inclusive workplaces so as to attract and retain more talented people, hence, it serves many purposes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: (In English): Companies that are positioning themselves for the upturn should plan ahead to ensure that they equip their workers with relevant skillsets after the temporary closure of workplace comes to an end.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Firms can tap on the enhanced support for redeployment programmes under the Adapt and Grow initiative to reskill their existing workers.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM has extended the funding period and introduced new redeployment programmes for the tourism, aviation, retail and food services sectors.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We wish to commend SITA and Orchard Hotel.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Despite the cost pressures, both companies decided to take a longer term perspective by holding onto their workers and helping the workers acquire new skills.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Employers who look after their staff are well placed to gain from their workers’ loyalty in the long run, especially when the upturn comes.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We call upon employers to help, to support and to care for their employees in this critical time.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We also call upon our employees to also do their part by understanding their employer’s situation.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: None of us is alone in this COVID-19 fight.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: MOM will continue to do our best to support employers and employees throughout this challenging period.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: Despite the unprecedented situation we face, we are confident that we can ride out the storm together.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: So, let us stay united, let us show our resilience and also stand in solidarity with one another because we Singaporeans, we are a tough lot.

speaker: The Senior Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister for Manpower (Ms Low Yen Ling)
text: We will not give up and we will prevail in this COVID-19 fight.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: I believe, for I choose to believe, that Singapore and Singaporeans have the gumption and mettle to ride this storm.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It will be a herculean effort, but we can – indeed, we must – do it.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: To	do	so,	we	need	to	face	reality	squarely	and	then chart our course to brighter days.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As	people play their part by staying at home, businesses suffer due to drop in demand.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Flights have almost come to a grinding halt as countries close their borders to contain and stabilise the spread of the COVID-19 virus.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Supply chains in certain sectors have been broken.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: With half of the world’s population mandated to stay at home as of Friday, 3 April, the world’s economy is almost at a standstill even as our medical forces show formidable courage, strength and resilience.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Besides implementing measures to “flatten the curve” and “break the circuit”, we must bolster our health force’s fight against the virus and should provide support for researchers and clinicians to find medical solutions to the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Such a debate is not just for the sake of those who contributed to our reserves, nor is it just for the sake of those whose sacrifices allowed us to have and preserve those reserves, but it is also for the sake of our younger generation and future generations yet to be born.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We must ensure for their sake that every dollar we spend from the reserves is a dollar deservedly spent.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In	that vein, I want to dive into four areas: one, aviation; two, tourism; three, rentals; four, supply chains.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: In particular, whether we are stretching every dollar in the Resilience Budget and the Solidarity Budget, so as to achieve optimum help in these areas.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The aviation sector is one of the industries in Singapore most affected by the COVID-19 crisis.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: It was one of the first to be impacted as travel restrictions were introduced by several countries early on to prevent cases from being imported.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: The impact was so severe that on 17 March this year, the Centre for Asia Pacific Aviation estimated that most of the world’s airlines will be bankrupt by end-May this year.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: As a travel hub, Singapore’s aviation industry is a key component, with our national carrier, Singapore Airlines, flying our	Singapore flag high.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: For Singapore	to continue to be	a	choice location	for regional headquarters, regional and international connectivity is crucial.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: We need to keep our aviation industry alive, so that	we	have a	strong,	supportive	and	connected eco-system for businesses to thrive in.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, I welcome the much needed support the Resilience Budget is giving to the aviation sector.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: But while these wages are being subsidised, the reality is our aircraft are grounded.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Therefore, one way in order to make the wage subsidy even more productive is to have the crew redeployed to sectors facing manpower shortages, for example, in the healthcare industry, or in companies needing to distribute medical devices such as respirators and ventilators.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: Quite possibly, this will be of relevance to the crew when eventually they fly again – having crew trained in emergency health skills is relevant to passenger aircraft.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
text: This makes SIA and its affiliated fleets more attractive when eventually they fly again.

speaker: Mr Christopher de Souza (Holland-Bukit Timah)
